source_title: Crash survivors recount chaos in Europe's worst train disaster since 2013
source_excerpt:
Passengers who survived a crash between two high-speed trains in central Spain were visibly emotional while being taken into the nearby village of Urda. ( AP: Andrea Comas )
Residents of a rural village in central Spain have rushed to help a massive emergency response after a crash involving two high-speed trains travelling between Madrid and Seville.
At least 68 people have died and dozens are injured.
Spain has declared three days of national mourning as investigations continue.
Residents of a rural village in central Spain have raced to provide help after Europe's deadliest rail disaster in more than a decade.
At least 68 people were killed and dozens more were injured when two high-speed trains carrying hundreds of passengers between Madrid and Seville collided in the Toledo province on Wednesday, local time.
A train operated by the state-owned RENFE company struck the rear of another train operated by private company IRYO that was stationery.
The collision derailed two carriages on the tail of the Iryo train and the front of the RENFE train.
The crash occurred on a flat stretch surrounded by olive fields between the villages of Urda and Los Yébenes, shredding carriages into bits of metal and other material.
Debris was scattered down a gravel slope.
Dozens of passengers were also injured in the crash and taken to an Urda sport centre converted into a triage treatment hub. ( AP: Andrea Comas )
In Urda, 78-year-old pharmacist Antonioa Garcia told Reuters he was among the first on the scene, jumping into his car to help after his daughter told him about the crash.
He said that as he neared the crash site, the scale of the accident became clear when he saw one carriage wedged inside another and scores of bodies.
Relatives of people who were aboard the train at the time of the crash travelled to the crash site in search of their family members. ( AP: Andrea Comas )
The pharmacist said he brought first-aid materials, painkillers and tranquillisers from his pharmacy, as well as blankets, to help treat the injured.
He also described how one passenger who had lost an arm in the crash was calmly asking for an ambulance, while another was saying his final goodbyes to his family.
The front carriage of one of the trains was severed after derailing following the collision. ( ABC News: Ryan Boyle )
"His last words were, 'God is good'. For those of us who are believers, these are very beautiful words," Mr Garcia said.
Other locals brought bottles of water to give to passengers who were evacuated from the two trains.
Construction worker David Gómez was also working nearby when he heard the crash and ran to help, he told the newspaper El País.
"People were trying to get out through the windows … We cut through some fences to access the area and treated people with the first-aid kits we had brought until emergency services arrived," he said.
"As I was trying to pull a young woman out, there was a piece of a leg."
The RENFE train rounded a bend in the railway leading up to the location of the stationary Iryo carriage. ( ABC News: Ryan Boyle )
Another survivor told reporters at the scene that he was standing close to a carriage door at the time of the crash.
"Passengers were breaking the glass to get out. Some people couldn't move because they were trapped among the seats," he said.
A visibly shaken Manuel Ortiz, who lives in Urda, told AFP he had been transporting survivors all morning in his car.
The two trains were derailed on either side of an embankment after the collision. ( AP: Manu Fernandez )
The 49-year-old described a "horrific, horrible" scene that "smelled of an accident, of metal".
Ambulances and medical helicopters made trips to and from the site, while buses took survivors who were unharmed. A military emergency brigade was deployed to help.
The crash is the second deadly rail incident in Spain since January, and the worst in Europe in more than a decade. ( AFP: Oscar Del Pozo )
Australian Education Minister Jason Clare said the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) was not aware of any Australians who had been affected by the crash.
"As you'd expect, we've got consular officials in Spain who stand ready to help any Australians or any Australian families if they are affected," he told the ABC.
"I think the whole country is in shock at the moment, seeing these images on our screens. [They're] just horrific."
In a statement, DFAT offered its condolences to victims' families and other people affected by the collision.
Samy Paul, a British tourist, was aboard the RENFE train at the time of the crash and described the shock of the impact to The Associated Press after being rescued.
"Suddenly, everything started falling apart. Bang! We fell down," he said.
"We realised carriage two, carriage one, all gone, all smashed. There was blood all over."
Members of the Spanish Red Cross helped to comfort family members of passengers who were waiting for news from the crash site. ( Reuters: Susana Vera )
Passenger Ignacio Relaño was also travelling on the RENFE train. He told state broadcaster TVE the train stopped momentarily on the line, then started again and crashed into the IRYO train.
"We all felt the train abruptly slowing down and then the impact," he said.
Pablo Mejia, 42, told AFP he had miraculously survived with injuries to his head after changing his seat.
With blood staining his grey jumper, he recounted "a very strong hit".
"It lasted a long time until it stopped, lots of people on the floor, on top of each other, seats ripped out, suitcases, a lot of chaos," he said.
A few hours after the crash, Urda was filled with police, firefighters and emergency workers from across the region, and the local sports hall was converted into a centre for survivors.
The local primary school was reserved for relatives of the victims, where a volunteer psychologist from Madrid named Carmen said she had been helping out since the morning.
"There were many mothers who found out their children had been killed," she said.
Some relatives made the two-hour trip from Madrid, the Spanish capital, to search for family members.
A woman who gave her name as Ana said she travelled to Urda after environmental police called to say they had found her dog, Trece, who was on board a train with her husband, Pepe.
Ana fought back tears as she described searching for her husband at the crash site, Urda's sports hall and the primary school, adding that his name was not on any list.
Expat journalist Chris Havler-Barrett told the ABC he had spent most of the day at the triage centre in Urda, which he described as "quite harrowing".
"[We] could hear the grief and cries of family who were receiving news on what must have been the worst day of their life," he said.
"It's an apocalyptic scene this country was not prepared for."
Mr Havler-Barrett said Spain's rail system was very busy at the time of the crash as people sought to travel before planned industrial action strikes on Thursday.
He also said the disaster occurred ahead of the busiest travel weekend of the year in Spain, as residents return home for All Saints Day.
Rescue workers continue to scour the wreckage of the two trains in search of survivors and bodies of victims.
The collision is the deadliest in Europe since a 2013 crash in Spain's Santiago de Compostela left 80 people dead.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has declared three days of national mourning and called for increased safety measures to restore confidence in the country's high-speed rail system.
